summary: Jesus leaves Galilee and resolutely sets out for Jerusalem; He rebukes James and John for wanting fire on a Samaritan village and tells would-be followers the cost.
key_insight: Luke marks the turning point of his Gospel by its goal: “the time had come for Him to be received up.” Jesus knew what waited in Jerusalem, and He “steadfastly set His face” toward it. From here to chapter 19, everything in Luke happens on the road to the cross.
story: When Jesus had finished His teaching, He departed from Galilee. {Mt} The time had come for Him to be received up, and He steadfastly set His face to go to Jerusalem. {Lk}

He sent messengers ahead of Him, and they went into a village of the Samaritans to prepare for Him. But the people there would not receive Him, because His face was set for the journey to Jerusalem. {Lk}

When James and John saw this, they said, “Lord, do You want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, just as Elijah did?” But Jesus turned and rebuked them: “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy men’s lives but to save them.” And they went on to another village. {Lk}

As they went along the road, a man said to Him, “Lord, I will follow You wherever You go.” Jesus answered, “Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.” To another He said, “Follow Me.” The man asked first to go and bury his father. Jesus said, “Let the dead bury their own dead, but you go and preach the kingdom of God.” {Lk}

Another said, “Lord, I will follow You, but let me first go and bid them farewell who are at my house.” Jesus said to him, “No one, having put his hand to the plow, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” {Lk}
So Jesus came into the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Great multitudes followed Him, and He healed them there. {Mt} And as He was accustomed, He taught them again. {Mk}
differences: Matthew and Mark say only that Jesus left Galilee and came to the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. Luke alone tells of the Samaritan village, James and John, and the three would-be followers.
Matthew says Jesus healed the crowds; Mark says He taught them, “as He was accustomed.”
Luke alone frames the journey with the time “for Him to be received up” and Jesus’ face set toward Jerusalem.

Matthew records two of the sayings to would-be followers much earlier, by the Sea of Galilee before the storm (Matthew 8:19–22). There the first man is a scribe, and Jesus answers the second, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”

fit.question: Luke places the would-be followers at the start of Jesus’ journey to Jerusalem. Matthew sets two of the same conversations much earlier, by the Sea of Galilee (Matthew 8:19–22). When did they happen?

points.label: Luke links loosely
points.text: Luke 9:51–19:27 reads as one long journey, but Luke joins its scenes loosely (“as they journeyed on the road,” 9:57) and gives no dates. He has Jesus in Martha’s village in 10:38, which John places just outside Jerusalem, yet still “journeying toward Jerusalem” in 13:22. He gathers teaching from these months along one road.

points.label: More than one volunteer
points.text: Jesus met many would-be followers. Matthew’s scribe and Luke’s volunteer may be different men given the same hard answer, and Luke records a third man Matthew does not mention.

points.label: Where Luke’s journey begins
points.text: Harmonies differ here too. McGarvey and Edersheim tie Luke 9:51 to Jesus’ trip to the Feast of Tabernacles (John 7:10), though John says that trip was made “as it were in secret,” while Luke has messengers going ahead. Others, followed in this timeline, place it with the final departure from Galilee (Matthew 19:1; Mark 10:1); on that view Jesus went north from Ephraim (John 11:54) before setting out.

fit.note: Luke never claims to give a day-by-day itinerary, so placing his scenes in time is a question for careful readers, not an error in the text.
fit.short: Luke arranges his journey loosely, without dates. Matthew may place the same conversation differently, or Jesus had a similar one on another day.

fit.question: Luke has Jesus heading into Samaria. Matthew and Mark say He came to Judea beyond the Jordan, east of the river. Which way did He go?

points.label: A refused route
points.text: Luke says only that the Samaritan village refused Him and “they went to another village” (9:56). Turned away, the company may well have taken the other road pilgrims used, down the Jordan valley through Perea, which is where Matthew and Mark say He came.

points.label: Along the border
points.text: Luke later says Jesus “passed through the midst of Samaria and Galilee” (17:11), most likely along the border between them, which fits a route heading east toward the Jordan.

fit.note: Luke tells how the journey began; Matthew and Mark tell where it led. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: Refused by a Samaritan village, Jesus went another way. Matthew and Mark tell where the road led: Judea beyond the Jordan.

scene.label: Two roads south
scene.text: Galilean pilgrims could go to Jerusalem straight through Samaria, about three days’ walk according to Josephus, or go down the Jordan valley on the east side, through Perea, and come up by Jericho. Josephus also tells of Galilean pilgrims attacked in Samaria on their way to a feast.

scene.label: Samaritans and Jerusalem
scene.text: Samaritans held that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, was the place to worship (John 4:20). A teacher whose face was set for the Jerusalem feast was not welcome to stay the night.

scene.label: Elijah’s fire
scene.text: James and John were thinking of 2 Kings 1:9–12, where Elijah called down fire on soldiers sent by the king who ruled from Samaria. Jesus had named these brothers “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17).

scene.label: Burial and the plow
scene.text: Burying a father was a sacred duty. The man may have meant his father had just died, or that he wanted to stay home until his father’s death; Luke does not say. The plow saying recalls Elisha, called from his plowing, who asked to kiss his parents goodbye before following Elijah (1 Kings 19:19–21).

scene.label: Words not in every manuscript
scene.text: Many of the oldest manuscripts do not have “just as Elijah did” (v. 54) or Jesus’ saying that begins “You do not know what manner of spirit you are of” (vv. 55–56). The NKJV includes them; many other translations place them in a footnote.

witnesses.matthew: Uses the phrase that closes each of his five great teaching sections: “when Jesus had finished these sayings” (compare 7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 26:1). The King’s teaching in Galilee is complete, and He turns toward Judea, still healing the great multitudes who follow Him.
witnesses.mark: Gives a single verse but adds that Jesus taught the crowds “as He was accustomed.” From here Mark’s story runs down the road to Jerusalem, with Jesus walking ahead of His amazed and fearful disciples (Mark 10:32).
witnesses.luke: Makes this the hinge of his Gospel. “Received up” looks beyond the cross to the Ascension, and the set face recalls the Servant who says, “I have set My face like a flint” (Isaiah 50:7). Luke, who also wrote Acts, later tells how John went to Samaria to pray for Samaritan believers to receive the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:14–17).

seeing.reveals: Jesus walks toward Jerusalem knowing what waits there, and neither rejection nor His disciples’ anger turns Him aside. He came to save lives, not to destroy them.
seeing.living: Jesus does not lower the cost to gain a follower. Following Him means putting His kingdom ahead of comfort and even family duty, without looking back. And those who follow a Savior whose face is set toward the cross cannot call down fire on the people who refuse Him.
seeing.ponder: What are you saying “first” about, before you will follow Jesus all the way?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus set His face toward the cross; He calls followers who will not look back.
preaching.watch_for: The word “face” frames the opening (vv. 51, 52, 53): Jesus sets His face, sends messengers before His face, and is refused because His face is set for Jerusalem. The section ends with a man looking back (v. 62); Jesus never does.
